modern:
Is there a church in this house? Are parents, children, friends and servants all members of it, or are some still unconverted? Let’s stop here and let the question go round the room: *Am I a member of the church in this house?* How father’s heart would leap for joy, and how mother’s eyes would fill with holy tears, if everyone from the oldest to the youngest were saved! Let’s pray for this great mercy until the Lord grants it to us.

Probably Philemon’s dearest wish had been to see his whole household saved, but at first it wasn’t granted to him in full. He had a wicked servant, Onesimus, who wronged him and ran away. His master’s prayers followed him, and at last, as God would have it, Onesimus was brought to hear Paul preach. His heart was touched, and he went back to Philemon, not only to be a faithful servant but a dearly loved brother, one more member of the church in Philemon’s house. Is an unconverted servant or child away from home this morning? Pray especially that when they come home, they’ll gladden every heart with good news of what grace has done! Is one here with us? Let him join in the same earnest prayer.

If there is a church like this in our house, let’s run it well, and let everyone act as in the sight of God. Let’s go about the ordinary business of life with careful holiness, hard work, kindness and integrity. More is expected of a church than of an ordinary household. In a home like that, family worship must be more devout and heartfelt, the love inside it must be warmer and unbroken, and its conduct toward the outside world must be holier and more like Christ. We don’t need to fear that being so few will strike us off the list of churches, for the Holy Spirit has written a family church here into the inspired book of remembrance. As a church, let’s now draw near to the great Head of the one universal Church, and ask him to give us grace to shine before people to the glory of his name.

notes.note: Paul greets Philemon, Apphia, Archippus “and to the church in thy house” ([[Phlm.1.2|Philemon 1:2]]). The first Christians met in homes.

The runaway whom Paul sent back to his master Philemon, “not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved” ([[Phlm.1.16|Philemon 1:16]]). The King James calls him a servant; he was a slave.
A humble, earnest request; a prayer.
An earnest request.
Careful, deliberate holiness, worked at on purpose.
“A book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD” ([[Mal.3.16|Malachi 3:16]]). Here, the Bible itself, which records this family church.
Draw near. “Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you” ([[Jas.4.8|James 4:8]]).

notes.term: The great head of the one Church universal
notes.note: Christ, “the head of the body, the church” ([[Col.1.18|Colossians 1:18]]).
Beg, ask earnestly.
“Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” ([[Matt.5.16|Matthew 5:16]]).

modern: The doom was universal; neither rich nor poor escaped. The educated and the uneducated, the admired and the hated, the religious and the irreverent, the old and the young all sank in one common ruin. No doubt some had mocked the patriarch: where are their merry jokes now? Others had threatened him for his zeal, which they took for madness: where are their boasts and harsh words now? The critic who judged the old man’s work is drowned in the same sea that covers his sneering friends. Those who spoke patronizingly of the good man’s loyalty to his convictions, but didn’t share them, have sunk never to rise again; and the workers who were paid to help build the wonderful ark are all lost too. The flood swept them *all* away, without a single exception. In the same way, outside of Christ, final destruction is certain for every man of woman born. No rank, possessions or character will be enough to save a single soul who hasn’t believed in the Lord Jesus. My soul, look at this sweeping judgment and tremble at it.

How amazing the general indifference was! They were all eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the awful morning dawned. There wasn’t one wise person on earth outside the ark. Folly fooled the whole human race: folly about saving themselves, the most foolish of all follies; folly in doubting the God who is perfectly true, the most spiteful foolishness of all. Strange, isn’t it, my soul? Everyone neglects their soul until grace gives them sense. Then they leave their madness behind and act like rational beings, but not until then.

*All* were safe in the ark, blessed be God; no ruin got in there. From the huge elephant down to the tiny mouse, all were safe. The timid hare was as secure as the brave lion, the helpless rock badger as safe as the hardworking ox. All are safe in Jesus. My soul, are you in him?

notes.term: Knew not until the flood came
notes.note: Jesus compares the day of his coming to the days of Noah ([[Matt.24.37-Matt.24.39|Matthew 24:37–39]]).
Noah. The patriarchs are the founding fathers of God’s people in Genesis.
Faithfulness, loyalty.
Not united to Christ by faith; outside him.
Every human being. “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble” ([[Job.14.1|Job 14:1]]).

notes.term: Eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage
notes.note: Jesus’ words for the ordinary life that went on right up to the flood ([[Matt.24.38|Matthew 24:38]]).
Fooled, tricked.
Spiteful, full of ill will.
The rock badger or hyrax, a small, timid animal: “The conies are but a feeble folk” ([[Prov.30.26|Proverbs 30:26]]).
Hardworking.

modern: It’s good for us that, amid all the ups and downs of life, there is One whom change can’t touch; One whose heart can never alter, and on whose brow the passing of time can leave no wrinkles. Everything else has changed, and everything is changing. The sun itself grows dim with age; the world is growing old; the folding up of the worn-out garment has begun; heaven and earth must soon pass away. They will perish; they will wear out like clothing. But there is One who alone is immortal, whose years have no end, and in whose person there is no change. The delight a sailor feels when, after being tossed about for many days, he steps onto solid ground again is the satisfaction a Christian feels when, amid all the changes of this troubled life, he rests the foot of his faith on this truth: “*I am the Lord, I change not*.”

The steadiness an anchor gives a ship when it has finally got a firm hold is like the steadiness the Christian’s hope gives him when it fastens on this glorious truth. With God “is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.” Whatever his attributes were long ago, they are now; his power, his wisdom, his justice and his truth are all unchanged. He has always been the refuge of his people, their stronghold in the day of trouble, and he is still their sure Helper. He is unchanged in his love. He has loved his people with “an everlasting love”; he loves them now as much as he ever did, and when everything on earth has melted in the last great fire, his love will still be as fresh as the dew of its youth. How precious it is to know for sure that he doesn’t change! The wheel of providence turns, but its axle is eternal love.

notes.term: I am the Lord, I change not
notes.note: [[Mal.3.6|Malachi 3:6]], which goes on: “therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.”

Growing old.

notes.note: A vesture is a garment. Of the heavens and the earth: “They shall perish… all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them” ([[Ps.102.25-Ps.102.27|Psalm 102:25–27]]; see also [[Heb.1.10-Heb.1.12|Hebrews 1:10–12]]).

A quality that belongs to God, such as his power or his love.

A conflagration is a great fire. Here, the burning up of the earth at the end: “the elements shall melt with fervent heat” ([[2Pet.3.10|2 Peter 3:10]]).
Freshness that never fades. “Thou hast the dew of thy youth” ([[Ps.110.3|Psalm 110:3]]).
Fades, grows less.

modern:
Prayer is the Christian’s never-failing resort in any situation, in every plight. When you can’t use your sword, you can turn to the weapon of all-prayer. Your gunpowder may be damp and your bowstring may have gone slack, but the weapon of all-prayer need never be out of order. Leviathan laughs at the javelin, but he trembles at prayer. Sword and spear need polishing, but prayer never rusts, and when we think it bluntest, it cuts best. Prayer is an open door that no one can shut. Devils may surround you on every side, but the way upward is always open, and as long as that road is clear, you won’t fall into the enemy’s hands. We can never be taken by blockade, by scaling ladder, by mine or by storm, as long as help from heaven can come down to us by Jacob’s ladder to relieve us in our time of need.

Prayer is never out of season: in summer and in winter alike, its goods are precious. Prayer gets an audience with heaven in the dead of night, in the middle of business, in the heat of noon, in the shadows of evening. Whatever your condition, whether poverty or sickness or obscurity or slander or doubt, your covenant God will welcome your prayer and answer it from his holy place.

Nor is prayer ever *futile*. True prayer is always true power. You may not always get what you ask for, but your real needs will always be met. When God doesn’t answer his children according to the letter, he answers according to the spirit. If you ask for coarse meal, will you be angry because he gives you the finest flour? If you ask for bodily health, should you complain if instead he makes your sickness work to heal the sicknesses of your soul? Isn’t it better to have the cross made holy than taken away? This evening, my soul, don’t forget to offer your prayer and request, for the Lord is ready to grant you your desires.

notes.term: Horror hath taken hold upon me
notes.note: The heading is [[Ps.119.53|Psalm 119:53]], but this edition prints the November 3 evening reading on prayer under it by mistake. Spurgeon’s own reading for tonight is on the holy horror a believer should feel at other people’s sin.
“Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit” ([[Eph.6.18|Ephesians 6:18]]), the last piece of the Christian’s armor in Ephesians 6.
Of the great sea creature in Job: “he laugheth at the shaking of a spear” ([[Job.41.29|Job 41:29]]).
Polishing; cleaning up a weapon.
Ways of taking a fortress: cutting off its supplies, climbing its walls with ladders, tunneling under them, or attacking head-on.
Help, relief; especially troops sent to rescue a town under siege.
The stairway reaching to heaven that Jacob saw in a dream, with angels going up and down on it ([[Gen.28.12|Genesis 28:12]]).
Always.

modern:
Prayers are noticed in heaven immediately. The moment Saul began to pray, the Lord heard him. Here is comfort for the soul that is distressed but praying. Often a poor brokenhearted person kneels but can only pour out his grief in sighs and tears; yet that groan has made all the harps of heaven thrill with music, and that tear has been caught by God and kept in heaven’s tear bottle. “Thou puttest my tears into thy bottle” implies that they are caught as they fall. The one praying, whose fears hold back his words, will be well understood by the Most High. He may only look up with misty eyes; but “prayer is the falling of a tear.” Tears are the diamonds of heaven; sighs are part of the music of Jehovah’s court, and are counted among “the sublimest strains that reach the majesty on high.” Don’t think that your prayer, however weak or trembling, will be ignored. Jacob’s ladder is tall, but our prayers will lean on the Angel of the covenant and so climb its starry rungs.

Our God not only *hears* prayer but *loves* to hear it. “He forgetteth not the cry of the humble.” True, he pays no attention to proud looks and lofty words; he cares nothing for the pomp and pageantry of kings; he doesn’t listen to the swell of military music; he takes no notice of human triumph and pride. But wherever there is a heart swollen with sorrow, or a lip quivering in agony, or a deep groan, or a sigh of repentance, the heart of Jehovah is open. He writes it down in the register of his memory. He puts our prayers, like rose petals, between the pages of his book of remembrance, and when the book is opened at last, a precious fragrance will rise from it.

notes.note: The Lord sends Ananias to Saul of Tarsus, blinded on the road to Damascus: “for, behold, he prayeth” ([[Acts.9.11|Acts 9:11]]).
A small bottle for tears. Bottles like this have been found in ancient tombs.

notes.term: Thou puttest my tears into thy bottle
notes.note: [[Ps.56.8|Psalm 56:8]]. Spurgeon quotes from memory; the King James reads “put thou my tears into thy bottle.”
Someone who prays humbly.

notes.term: Prayer is the falling of a tear
notes.note: From James Montgomery’s hymn “Prayer is the soul’s sincere desire”: “Prayer is the burden of a sigh, the falling of a tear.”

notes.term: The sublimest strains that reach the majesty on high
notes.note: From the same hymn, which says prayer is both the simplest speech a child can manage and the loftiest music that reaches God.
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
The stairway reaching to heaven that Jacob saw in a dream ([[Gen.28.12|Genesis 28:12]]).
Christ. Malachi foretells “the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in” ([[Mal.3.1|Malachi 3:1]]); the Hebrew word for messenger also means angel.
The rungs of a ladder.

modern:
One of the first qualifications for serving God with any success at all, for doing God’s work well and triumphantly, is a sense of our own weakness. When God’s warrior marches out to battle strong in his own strength, when he boasts, “I know I’ll win; my own right arm and my conquering sword will win me the victory,” defeat isn’t far off. God won’t go out with the man who marches in his own strength. Whoever counts on victory that way has miscounted, for “it is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.” Those who go out to fight boasting of their prowess will come back with their bright banners dragged in the dust and their armor stained with disgrace. Those who serve God must serve him in his own way and in his strength, or he will never accept their service. Whatever people do without God’s strength, God can never own. He throws away the mere fruits of the earth; he will only harvest the grain whose seed was sown from heaven, watered by grace and ripened by the sun of God’s love.

God will empty out everything you have before he puts his own into you; he will first clear out your barns before he fills them with the finest of the wheat. The river of God is full of water, but not one drop of it flows from earthly springs. God will have no strength used in his battles except the strength he himself gives. Are you mourning over your own weakness? Take courage, for there must be an awareness of weakness before the Lord will give you victory. Your emptiness is only the preparation for your being filled, and your being cast down is only the making ready for your being lifted up.

notes.term: My strength is made perfect in weakness
notes.note: The Lord’s answer when Paul prayed three times for his “thorn in the flesh” to be taken away ([[2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.9|2 Corinthians 12:7–9]]).

modern:
No lips can tell the heart about the love of Christ until Jesus himself speaks within. All descriptions fall flat and tame unless the Holy Spirit fills them with life and power; until our Immanuel reveals himself inside, the soul doesn’t see him. If you wanted to see the sun, would you gather up all the ordinary lamps and try to see the great light of day by them? No, the wise person knows that the sun must reveal itself, and that mighty lamp can only be seen by its own blaze. It’s the same with Christ. “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona:” he said to Peter, “for flesh and blood hath not revealed this unto thee.” Refine flesh and blood by any kind of education you like, raise the mind to the highest pitch of intellectual power, and still none of these can reveal Christ. The Spirit of God must come with power and overshadow a person with his wings, and then, in that mysterious holy of holies, the Lord Jesus must show himself to the eye that has been made holy, as he doesn’t to the half-blind children of men. Christ must be his own mirror.

The great mass of this bleary-eyed world can see nothing of Immanuel’s glories, which are beyond words. He stands before them with no form or beauty, a root out of dry ground, rejected by the shallow and despised by the proud. Only where the Spirit has touched the eye with eye salve, made the heart alive with God’s life and trained the soul to a heavenly taste, only there is he understood. “To you that believe he is precious”; to you he is the chief cornerstone, the Rock of your salvation, your all in all; but to others he is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence.” Happy are those to whom our Lord reveals himself, for his promise to them is that he will *make his home with them*. O Jesus, our Lord, our heart is open: come in, and never go out again. Show yourself to us now! Grant us a glimpse of your all-conquering beauty.

modern: This day stands out in English history for two great rescues God worked for us. On this day in 1605, the Roman Catholics’ plot to blow up our Houses of Parliament was discovered.
And second, today is the anniversary of King William III’s landing at Torbay in 1688, which crushed the hope of Roman Catholic rule and made religious liberty secure.

This day should be celebrated, not by the wild partying of boys, but by the songs of saints. Our Puritan forefathers kept it, with deep devotion, as a special time of thanksgiving. A record still survives of the sermons Matthew Henry preached on this day every year. Our Protestant feeling and our love of liberty should make us keep its anniversary with holy gratitude. Let our hearts and lips cry out, “We have heard with our ears, and our fathers have told us the wondrous things which thou didst in their day, and in the old time before them.” You have made this nation the home of the gospel, and when the enemy has risen against her, you have shielded her. Help us to offer repeated songs for repeated rescues. Give us more and more a hatred of Antichrist, and hurry on the day when she is wiped out entirely. Until then, and always, we believe the promise, “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper.” On this day, shouldn’t every lover of the gospel of Jesus feel moved to plead for false teaching to be overthrown and God’s truth to spread? Wouldn’t it be good to search our own hearts, and throw out any Roman Catholic junk of self-righteousness that may be hidden there?

notes.term: No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper

notes.note: Spurgeon’s word, common among Protestants of his day, for Roman Catholics.

notes.term: The plot… to destroy our Houses of Parliament
notes.note: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605, when a group of Catholic conspirators, Guy Fawkes among them, planned to blow up Parliament with King James I inside. It was discovered the night before.
The Dutch Protestant prince William of Orange landed at Torbay in Devon on November 5, 1688. The Catholic king James II fled, and William and his wife Mary took the throne.
Roman Catholic rule. “Popish” was a hostile Protestant word for Roman Catholic.
The rowdy fun of boys on Guy Fawkes Night, with bonfires, fireworks and burning straw “guys”. Saturnalia was a wild Roman festival; striplings are youths.

The papacy, as Spurgeon and many Protestants of his day saw it. The “her” follows their reading of the woman called Babylon in [[Rev.17.5|Revelation 17]] as the church of Rome.

modern: Our Lord wants all his people to be rich in high and happy thoughts about his blessed person. Jesus isn’t content for his brothers and sisters to think little of him; it is his pleasure that his bride should delight in his beauty. We aren’t to think of him as a bare necessity, like bread and water, but as a luxury, a rare and thrilling delight. To this end he has revealed himself as the “pearl of great price” in its matchless beauty, as the “bundle of myrrh” in its refreshing fragrance, as the “rose of Sharon” in its lasting perfume, and as the “lily” in its spotless purity.

To help you think highly of Christ, remember how highly he is valued beyond the skies, where things are measured by the right standard. Think how God values his Only Begotten, his gift to us that is beyond words. Consider what the angels think of him, as they count it their highest honor to veil their faces at his feet. Consider what the blood-washed think of him, as day and night they sing the praises he so well deserves. High thoughts of Christ will help us act in keeping with our relationship to him. The more loftily we see Christ enthroned, and the more humbly we bow at the foot of the throne, the better prepared we’ll be to play our part toward him. Our Lord Jesus wants us to think well of him so that we’ll submit cheerfully to his authority. High thoughts of him increase our love; love and high regard go together.

So, believer, think much about your Master’s excellences. Study him in his glory before time began, before he took your nature on himself! Think of the mighty love that drew him from his throne to die on the cross! Admire him as he conquers all the powers of hell! See him risen, crowned, glorified! Bow before him as the Wonderful, the Counselor, the mighty God, for only then will your love for him be what it should be.

modern:
When a believer has fallen into a low, sad state of mind, he often tries to lift himself out of it by punishing himself with dark and gloomy fears. That isn’t the way to rise from the dust, but to stay in it. You might as well chain the eagle’s wing to make it fly as doubt in order to grow in grace. It isn’t the law but the gospel that saves the seeking soul at first, and it isn’t legal slavery but gospel freedom that can restore the fainting believer afterward. Slavish fear doesn’t bring the backslider back to God, but the sweet wooing of love draws him to Jesus’ heart.

Are you thirsting for the living God this morning, and unhappy because you can’t find him to your heart’s delight? Have you lost the joy of your faith, and is this your prayer: “Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation”? Are you also aware that you are barren, like dry ground; that you aren’t producing the fruit for God that he has a right to expect from you; that you aren’t as useful in the church or in the world as your heart longs to be? Then here is exactly the promise you need: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty.” You’ll receive the grace you need so badly, and you’ll have it to the furthest reach of your needs. Water refreshes the thirsty: you’ll be refreshed; your desires will be satisfied. Water wakes up sleeping plant life: your life will be woken by fresh grace. Water swells the buds and ripens the fruit: you’ll have fruit-bearing grace; you’ll be made fruitful in God’s ways. Whatever good quality there is in God’s grace, you’ll enjoy it to the full. You’ll receive all the riches of God’s grace in plenty; you’ll be drenched with it, so to speak. And just as meadows are sometimes flooded when the rivers burst their banks, and the fields turn into pools, so it will be with you: the thirsty land will become springs of water.

modern:
There is a strange power in the very word “blood”, and the sight of it always moves us. A kind heart can’t bear to see a sparrow bleed, and unless it’s hardened by habit, it turns away in horror at the slaughter of an animal. As for human blood, it’s a sacred thing: shedding it in anger is murder, and wasting it in war is a dreadful crime. Is this solemn feeling caused by the fact that the blood is the life, and pouring it out is the sign of death? We think so. When we rise to think about the blood of the Son of God, our awe grows even greater, and we shudder as we think of the guilt of sin and the terrible penalty the Sin-bearer endured. Blood, always precious, is priceless when it streams from Immanuel’s side.

The blood of Jesus seals the *covenant* of grace and makes it forever sure. Covenants in ancient times were made by sacrifice, and the everlasting covenant was ratified the same way. Oh, the joy of being saved on the sure foundation of God’s own commitments, which can never be dishonored! Salvation by the works of the law is a fragile, broken ship, sure to be wrecked; but the covenant ship fears no storms, for the blood makes the whole of it secure. The blood of Jesus made his *testament*, his will, valid. A will has no force unless the one who made it dies. In this light the soldier’s spear is a blessed help to faith, since it proved that our Lord was really dead. There can be no doubt about that, and we may boldly claim the legacies he has left for his people. Happy are those who see their right to heaven’s blessings secured for them by a dying Savior. But does this blood have nothing to say to us? Doesn’t it tell us to set ourselves apart for the one who redeemed us? Doesn’t it call us to new life, and urge us to give ourselves wholly to the Lord? Oh, that we might know and feel the power of the blood in us tonight!

modern:
No doubt part of the wonder packed into the word “*Behold*” is stirred up by the unbelieving complaint in the sentence before it. Zion said, “The Lord hath forsaken me, and my God hath forgotten me.” How amazed the mind of God seems to be at this wicked unbelief! What could be more astonishing than the groundless doubts and fears of God’s favored people? The Lord’s loving word of rebuke should make us blush. He cries, “How could I have forgotten you, when I have engraved you on the palms of my hands? How dare you doubt that I constantly remember you, when the reminder is cut into my very flesh?” Oh, unbelief, what a strange wonder you are! We don’t know which to wonder at more, the faithfulness of God or the unbelief of his people. He keeps his promise a thousand times, and yet the next trial makes us doubt him. He never fails; he is never a dry well; he is never like a setting sun, a passing meteor or a melting mist; and yet we are as constantly troubled with worries, harassed with suspicions and disturbed with fears as if our God were the mirage of the desert.

“Behold” *is a word meant to stir up wonder*. Here, indeed, we have something to marvel at. Heaven and earth may well be astonished that rebels should come so near to the heart of infinite love as to be written on the palms of his hands. “I have graven *thee*.” It doesn’t say, “Thy name.” The name is there, but that isn’t all: “I have graven *thee*.” See how full this is! I have engraved your person, your likeness, your situation, your circumstances, your sins, your temptations, your weaknesses, your needs, your works. I have engraved you, everything about you, all that concerns you; I have put the whole of you there. Will you ever say again that your God has forsaken you, when he has engraved you *on* his own palms?

modern:
To learn how to do your duty as a witness for Christ, look at his example. He is always witnessing: by the well of Samaria or in the temple at Jerusalem, by the lake of Gennesaret or on the mountainside. He witnesses night and day; his mighty prayers speak to God as clearly as his daily work. He witnesses in every situation: scribes and Pharisees can’t shut his mouth; even before Pilate he witnesses a good confession. He witnesses so clearly and distinctly that there’s no mistaking him.

Christian, make your life a clear testimony. Be like the brook where you can see every stone on the bottom, not like the muddy creek where you only see the surface. Be clear and transparent, so that your heart’s love for God and for people is visible to everyone. You don’t need to say, “I am true”: be true. Don’t boast of integrity; be upright. Then your testimony will be such that people can’t help seeing it. Never hold back your witness for fear of feeble man. Your lips have been warmed with a coal from the altar; let them speak the way lips touched by heaven should. “In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand.” Don’t watch the clouds or check the wind. In season and out of season, witness for the Savior. And if it happens that for Christ’s sake and the gospel’s you must suffer in any form, don’t shrink back, but rejoice in the honor this gives you, that you are counted worthy to suffer with your Lord. Be glad of this too: your sufferings, losses and persecutions will make you a platform from which you’ll witness for Christ Jesus all the more vigorously and powerfully. Study your great Example, and be filled with his Spirit. Remember that you need much teaching, much upholding, much grace and much humility if your witnessing is to bring glory to your Master.
